questions.q: According to the NCERT text, what are the two senses in which the word 'partial' is used to describe common sense knowledge about society?
questions.a: The two senses are: (1) incomplete (the opposite of whole) — common sense sees only a part of social reality; (2) biased (the opposite of impartial) — it is tilted toward the viewpoints and interests of one's own social group. A wrong answer that mentions only 'biased' or only 'incomplete' reveals the student has not grasped the dual meaning NCERT emphasises, which is crucial for understanding why unlearning is necessary.

questions.q: A student says: "I don't need to study sociology because I already know Indian society — I'm Indian!" Using the concept of 'unlearning', explain why this student's confidence is exactly the problem sociology addresses.
questions.a: The student's confidence comes from common sense acquired through socialization into a specific group (family, region, class, caste). This knowledge is 'partial' — incomplete and biased — because it reflects only their group's viewpoint. Sociology requires unlearning this taken-for-granted knowledge to see society from multiple, systematic perspectives. A wrong answer that says 'common sense is wrong' misses the point: common sense is not necessarily false, but partial; unlearning is about expanding vision, not just correcting errors.

questions.q: Riya, a Class 12 student from an upper-middle-class urban family, worries she won't get into a good college because her marks are average. Using C. Wright Mills' distinction, identify this as a 'personal trouble' and then reformulate it as a 'social issue' by naming at least two structural factors in Indian society that shape college admissions.
questions.a: Personal trouble: Riya's individual anxiety about her marks and future. Social issue: The structural mismatch between the number of quality higher-education seats and the aspirant population; the role of coaching industries that favour economically privileged students; caste-based reservation policies that redistribute seats; regional disparities in school quality. A wrong answer that lists only 'competition' or 'population' without naming specific Indian structural mechanisms (reservation, coaching economy, regional inequality) shows inability to connect biography to history and social structure.

questions.q: Compare and contrast 'self-reflexivity' in sociology with 'introspection' in psychology. Why does the NCERT text insist that sociological self-reflexivity must be 'critical — quick to criticise and slow to praise oneself'?
questions.a: Introspection in psychology examines internal mental states; sociological self-reflexivity examines one's social location (class, caste, gender, religion, region) and how it shapes one's view of society. The 'critical' stance is required because our social position gives us unearned advantages or blind spots; uncritical self-praise reinforces the very partiality sociology seeks to overcome. A wrong answer that equates self-reflexivity with 'thinking about myself' misses the structural, outward-looking dimension: it is about seeing oneself as a social actor positioned in a web of power relations.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "Studying Indian sociology is only useful for students who want to become sociologists; for engineers, doctors, or business students, it is a waste of time." Use the concepts of social map and sociological imagination in your evaluation.
questions.a: The claim is flawed. Every professional operates within Indian society: engineers design for diverse users (caste, gender, disability access); doctors encounter health disparities shaped by poverty, caste, gender; business students must understand consumer behaviour across religious, regional, linguistic lines. The social map locates every professional in networks of power and privilege; the sociological imagination helps them see how personal career troubles (e.g., workplace discrimination, market failure) connect to social issues (patriarchy, regional inequality). A wrong answer that says 'it builds general awareness' without linking to professional practice misses the instrumental value of sociological tools for any citizen-professional.

questions.q: Create a 'social map' for a fictional 18-year-old character from a background very different from your own (specify: region, language, caste/tribe, class, religion, gender). Then write one 'personal trouble' this character might face and trace it to a 'social issue' using at least two structural factors from Indian society.
questions.a: Example: Character — Adivasi girl from Bastar, Chhattisgarh; Halbi speaker; Gond tribe; Below Poverty Line; animist/Christian; female. Personal trouble: She drops out of school after Class 8. Social issue: Structural factors — (1) Lack of schools in conflict-affected tribal areas (state neglect, militarisation); (2) Gendered division of labour and early marriage norms in her community; (3) Medium of instruction (Hindi/English) alien to her language. A poor answer creates a stereotypical character or lists only individual factors (laziness, lack of interest) without structural analysis, showing failure to apply the sociological imagination.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The ______ of a sociology of India lies in its systematic, scientific study of Indian society that moves beyond common sense by requiring 'unlearning' of partial, group-biased knowledge, enabling self-reflexivity (critical examination of one's own social location), and connecting personal troubles to broader social issues through the sociological imagination.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you are asked: "Why do we need a whole subject to study Indian society when we live in it every day?" Start by listing three things you 'know' about Indian society (e.g., 'joint ______ are breaking down', 'caste doesn't matter in cities', 'youth are westernised').
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain why common sense is inadequate for studying society, define self-reflexivity and the sociological imagination in their own words, and apply these concepts to analyse a personal experience as a social issue rooted in structural features of Indian society.
